absent: Numeric values of MP bus, interrupt type and flag constants and MADT type codes.
Full layouts of boot_params, x86_init, mpc tables, dmi match encoding and e820 capacity.
Semantics of firmware table parsers, GSI translation, APIC and pin lookup, IRQ count helpers and route saving.
Exact effects of firmware flags for force, strict, noirq, SCI override, timer override and reduced hardware outside shown assignments.
Behavior of PCI firmware init, SPCR console, HPET, BGRT, multiprocessor wakeup and Xen domain helpers.
Concurrency and lifetime rules for firmware memory map and interrupt route tables beyond shown serialization.
Complete DMI matching semantics and full board quirk coverage.

findings.text: Early boot first checks board quirks and locates initial firmware tables, then completes table setup, consults blacklist with force override, processes processor interrupt description early and applies reduced hardware adjustment; full boot repeats late quirks and firmware parsing for boot, fixed description, interrupt description, timer and graphics tables, then wires PCI routing unless IRQ routing disabled and registers firmware console.

Processor interrupt description handling has early and full phases: early attempts address override and marks local APIC and multiprocessor config found on success; full parses local entries then input-output entries under serialization and marks multiprocessor config and input-output IRQ model on success, with invalid description disabling firmware support and missing description clearing multiprocessor config.

Input-output APIC enumeration is gated on firmware enabled, IRQ routing allowed, local APIC present and probe not disabled; on success it collects APIC units, source overrides, ensures a system-control interrupt entry unless reduced hardware, fills identity legacy mappings, then collects nonmaskable sources, propagating failures with logged diagnostics.

Legacy ISA interrupts are identity mapped from ISA number to firmware global number and APIC pin with conforming type, skipping numbers lacking translation or APIC owner and skipping duplicates already covered by same bus number or same destination pin.
An alternate build provides an input-output enumeration routine that always reports failure, representing configurations without that support.
Full interrupt description processing holds the firmware input-output serialization mutex only around the input-output enumeration phase.

Firmware global lock handoff uses repeated atomic read and compare exchange on a shared word, updating low arbitration bits to request ownership and observe pending state without blocking, with acquire and release reporting prior pending and ownership indications.

Boot parameters select firmware disable, forced enable despite blacklist, strict handling, table flavor, IRQ routing disable, local table copy, firmware error mode adjustment and console preference, plus separate controls for graphics table use, PCI firmware routing, timer override behavior and system-control interrupt trigger and polarity.

Board quirk tables pair vendor and product and BIOS identity patterns with actions that disable firmware, IRQ routing, PCI firmware use, extended table use or timer override handling, honoring forced enable and ending with an empty terminator.

Hardware reduced mode replaces timer and pre-vector initialization with no-ops and substitutes a null legacy interrupt controller, activated through an early indirection when the reduced hardware flag is set.

An invalid processor interrupt description disables firmware support, while absence of that description when multiprocessor config was previously found clears the multiprocessor flag to force single-processor programmable interrupt mode.

On builds with local APIC but without multiprocessor table parsing, disabling firmware or its IRQ routing triggers a warning and failure indication, except for paravirtual guests that are not initial domains.
An interrupt route record carries source bus and bus IRQ, destination APIC identity and pin, plus type, trigger flags and category fields used to express conforming identity mappings.
A firmware memory record holds base address, length and usage type; the table holds a bounded array of such records with a count, normalized via transient boundary and overlap helpers.
A board quirk record holds a callback, a short identity label and a list of field matches over system, board and BIOS strings.
Appending a firmware memory range succeeds when table capacity remains and otherwise logs and discards the new range.

Memory map normalization ignores empty ranges, rejects address wrap, orders all start and end boundaries, sweeps them tracking active ranges with highest usage value winning overlaps, emits new spans on type change subject to merge rules, then replaces the table contents.
PRAM and soft reserved usage types never coalesce across adjacent spans to preserve platform boundaries, while all other types may merge.
An architecture helper records a firmware nonvolatile range in the memory map and refreshes the consolidated map printout.

Map printing reports out of order entries and gaps between ranges, then logs each range with its usage label, distinguishing system RAM, reserved, soft reserved, firmware data, nonvolatile, unusable, persistent variants and unknown numeric types.
Boot time firmware table setup, early and full boot initialization, reduced hardware setup and multiprocessor compatibility check are exposed for initial boot sequencing.

Memory range addition, map normalization and print refresh, firmware nonvolatile reservation, firmware root pointer access and global lock acquire and release are exposed for boot and firmware interaction.
Firmware root table address is stored in and retrieved from boot parameters through a paired setter and getter.
Firmware boot control is selected by discrete keywords for disable, force, strict, table flavor, IRQ routing, table copy, error handling and console use.
System control interrupt boot control accepts separate trigger choices of edge or level and polarity choices of high or low, each preserving the complementary field.
Legacy mapping silently omits interrupts without firmware translation or without owning APIC to avoid incomplete routes.
Normalization leaves the table unchanged for trivial maps or address errors and stops emitting when new entry capacity exhausts.
